summary:
Is the Mediterranean turning tropical?

As Earth's climate trends change, habitats change too. We're turning climate data into biodiversity insights, helping us understand the future of life on our planet. The Nautilus Engine is an advanced interactive platform designed to quantify and visualize these ecological shifts.

To investigate how marine life is responding to a changing ocean, we integrate two massive databases: NASA climate records (GIOVANNI, MERRA-2, MODIS-Aqua) and global species sightings from OBIS. First, we analyze decades of NASA data to isolate proven ocean trends, such as shifting surface temperatures and chlorophyll levels. Next, we cross-reference this with OBIS to extract the specific environmental ranges where a chosen species typically lives.

While real-world survival depends on a highly complex web of factors beyond our scope, analyzing these fundamental metrics provides a robust baseline to define a species' Environmental Suitability Area.

By intersecting climate history with biological records, The Nautilus Engine generates dynamic, year-by-year maps. We don't just show that the sea is changing—we visualize exactly how those physical changes are actively redrawing ecological boundaries.
details:
The Nautilus Engine is an analytical platform that quantifies how climate change is actively shifting marine habitats.

How it works: It operates through a three-stage computational pipeline:

  • Trend Extraction (Physical): We process historical Earth observation data (1980–present). To separate true climate signals from background noise, we apply rigorous statistical filtering using Sen's slope estimator and the modified Mann-Kendall test (with False Discovery Rate adjustment).
  • Niche Modeling (Biological): We query the OBIS API for global species occurrence coordinates. By intersecting these sightings with historical climate grids, we extract the baseline environmental tolerances (the fundamental niche) for specific marine species.
  • Suitability Synthesis: The engine merges these datasets to compute the Environmental Suitability Area (ESA). It renders dynamic, year-by-year spatial maps that visualize how habitat boundaries are migrating over time.

Tools and Data Sources:

  • NASA Datasets: MERRA-2 (heat fluxes, atmospheric data via GES DISC), MODIS-Aqua (chlorophyll via NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP), SMAP (salinity via PO.DAAC), and GIOVANNI (historical variable extraction).
  • Biological Data: Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS) API.
  • Frontend & Visualization: Built with HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript. We utilized the HTML5 Canvas API to ensure high-performance rendering of complex spatial maps, time-series graphs, and climate stripes directly in the browser.
  • Backend: Python.
  • Infrastructure: Server running on Google Cloud.
  • Development Tools: AI assistance was used to optimize JavaScript algorithms, generate statistical functions, and streamline the UI architecture.

Impact and Key Benefits:

  • Ecological Forecasting: Enables researchers to hypothesize invasive species pathways and track potential habitat loss for endemic species.
  • Data Translation: Converts abstract, terabyte-scale climate datasets into actionable, visually intuitive biological boundaries.
  • Reproducibility: Provides a transparent, statistically rigorous framework that can be applied to any marine region or species globally.

Creativity and Innovation:

Our primary innovation is cross-disciplinary data fusion. Rather than simply plotting sea surface temperatures, we built an engine that translates physical oceanography into biological impact. We embraced the "Detective" prompt by starting with 22 candidate environmental variables and rigorously filtering them down to the 4 most critical drivers of marine distribution.

Key Factors Considered (Scientific Integrity):

A major factor we addressed was biological complexity. Ecosystems are governed by countless variables (predation, food webs, pollution) that cannot be perfectly modeled by a few metrics. To maintain scientific validity, our model explicitly avoids claiming absolute "survivability." Instead, we define the Environmental Suitability Area—providing a robust physical baseline of where a species could live, acknowledging that physical climate trends are the primary architects of marine habitats.
dataRefs: NASA MERRA-2 monthly single-level diagnostics (M2TMNXSLV) — sea surface temperature
NASA MERRA-2 monthly surface flux diagnostics (M2TMNXFLX) — wind, evaporation, heat fluxes
NASA MERRA-2 monthly aerosol diagnostics (M2TMNXAER) — aerosol optical depth
NASA GES DISC — MERRA-2 data archive
NASA MODIS-Aqua Ocean Color — chlorophyll-a and fluorescence
NASA SMAP sea surface salinity — PO.DAAC
NASA Giovanni — time series API, used in the exploratory phase
NASA Earthdata OPeNDAP — data access used by the pipeline
projectRefs: NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP — server used to access NASA MODIS-Aqua monthly data
